name: Athenian Democracy
summary: Athenian democracy was direct rule by the adult male citizens, who met in the Assembly, filled most offices by lot and judged cases in large popular courts. It prized equality among citizens, free debate and public service, while excluding women, slaves and resident foreigners and holding an empire of subject states for much of the fifth century BC.
scope: Classical Athens from the reforms of Cleisthenes and Ephialtes through Pericles to the restored democracy of the fourth century BC, based on Pericles' Funeral Oration in Thucydides, Aristotle's Athenian Constitution and modern reference works. Excludes modern democratic theory and later revivals.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Athens policed the grain trade through magistrates and anti-hoarding rules because the city depended on imported grain; this is from general knowledge of the period and is not confirmed in the cited pages.

party-controls-media.rationale: Athens had no ruling party or press, and the Funeral Oration praises open debate and freedom in public life, so adherents would reject government control of information; inferred from that ethos.

party-commands-army.rationale: Athens had no parties; the citizen militia and fleet were led by generals elected by and answerable to the Assembly, so command by a party rather than the citizen body would be foreign; inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship was tightly guarded (descent from Athenian parents, grants of citizenship rare and voted by the Assembly), so a long wait fits the spirit, though Athens had no residence path at all; inferred.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay for office and jury service let poorer citizens serve, and officials were ordinary citizens chosen by lot, though pay was a day wage rather than a stated cap.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Athens had no parties and prized free debate in the Assembly, so binding members would cut against its practice.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Inferred: Athens ran an empire of subject states under its own control and prized citizen self-rule, not sharing decisions in a binding union.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The sovereign Assembly decided war and policy, and the generals who commanded forces were elected and held to account by it; there was no head of state.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Athenian religion was civic, run by magistrates and citizen priesthoods, with no bishops or church hierarchy.

clerical-rule.rationale: Political authority rested with the citizen Assembly and courts; priests had no governing role.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration calls on citizens to put the city first and die for it, and the citizens themselves were the government.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Inferred from Pericles' praise of free discussion and open comic theatre, though Athens did prosecute impiety, as in Plato's criticism.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Most offices were held once by lot, but generals such as Pericles were re-elected repeatedly; adherents would be split.

recall-officials.rationale: Officials were scrutinized before and after office, could be deposed or impeached by the Assembly, and ostracism removed leaders by vote.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Inferred: Athens led an alliance and empire that kept its forces abroad, so adherents would not withdraw from alliances.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Inferred: not addressed; resident foreigners rented homes and citizens held land, and nothing suggests Athenians wanted to ban renting.

people-in-arms.rationale: Athenian citizens served as soldiers and rowers themselves; Pericles boasts that Athens relies on its own citizens rather than on drilled foreign methods.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Not addressed; Pericles praises the city and many Athenians lived in the countryside, so adherents are split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Not addressed; adherents of the polis had no doctrine on reunifying divided peoples.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Inferred: Pericles says Athenians cultivate the mind without losing practical action and that ordinary citizens judge policy well, so the educated are not set apart.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Inferred: Pericles calls Athens the school of Hellas, and Greeks regarded their culture as above that of outsiders.

death-penalty.rationale: Inferred: Athenian popular courts imposed the death penalty for grave crimes, and nothing in the democracy opposes it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Anachronistic; Athenian women were excluded from public life and there was no school curriculum of this kind.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not addressed; civic religion was central but there were no school curricula or creation doctrine, so adherents have no clear view.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred: Athenian art and comedy were largely free of state restriction on erotic content, though not the subject of political doctrine.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Athens limited citizenship to those with Athenian parents, as the citizenship rules recorded in Aristotle and reference works show.

minority-language-support.rationale: Inferred: public business was conducted in Greek by the citizen body, and no support for other languages is recorded.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Inferred: the democracy enforced civic religion through impiety prosecutions and applied the same laws to all citizens.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Pericles says Athens does not frown on a neighbour for living as he pleases, so private diversity is welcomed, though adherents would not make it a goal.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Athens' Solonian tradition of shaking off debts suggests sympathy for relief, but it was domestic, so foreign-debt cancellation is inferred.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Anachronistic; Athenians defended polis independence but did not tie it to property transformation.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The sovereign Assembly and legislative boards (nomothetai) rewrote laws and constitutions, as in the 403 BC revision.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Athenian democrats prized free speech and equal participation, as in the Funeral Oration; inferred against suspending them.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Duties ran to citizens and the empire extracted tribute; global aid is inferred as foreign to the ethos.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Athens prized self-reliant defence of the polis; inferred, as nuclear weapons are anachronistic.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Democrats saw sortition, not elections, as the democratic method and elections as favouring the wealthy; there was no single head of state.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Public finance was controlled by the Assembly and councils; insulating money from popular rule is inferred as alien.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Not addressed; Athens' practice varied by circumstance.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Wealth was expected to serve the city through liturgies and Pericles praises public use of means, though private property was protected; inferred.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Anachronistic and not an Athenian question.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Ancient Athens had no concept of environmental risk, so it is left neutral as an inference.

collective-defense.rationale: Athens built its power on alliances such as the Delian League and defended allies, as the Funeral Oration's pride in aiding friends suggests; inferred.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Athens held an empire of subject states and settled its citizens on conquered land, so adherents would not call such control unlawful occupation.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Athenian religion was run by the polis, with magistrates overseeing sacrifices and festivals, so priests served the state; inferred.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Athens had no head of state, only annual officials chosen by lot or vote; the role is not applicable.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Athens suppressed revolts by allies such as Naxos and Thasos, and Pericles says the empire could not safely be let go.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Athens first let League members keep their own systems and later imposed its own; adherents are split.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Athens abolished kingship and held that power belonged to the citizens, so a divine ruler is alien to it.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Athens funded public needs through liturgies and levies on the wealthy rather than an equal rate; inferred.

character-from-environment.rationale: Athenian thought, including the Sophists, stressed both teaching and nature; no firm position.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Pericles says Athenians obey the laws, and Athens held its officials accountable under law, so no ruler was above it.

space-expansion.rationale: Not addressed in ancient Athens; inferred as indifferent.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Athenian democrats ruled through the Assembly, lot and popular courts, and rejected oligarchic or aristocratic elements.

leader-cult.rationale: Athens used ostracism to check over-mighty individuals and shunned tyranny, so mass cults of a leader were alien to it.

equal-parenting.rationale: Athenian law gave a father's household control of his children, so equal time for both parents is not supported; inferred.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Class conflict between rich and poor was a feature of Athenian politics, but socialism did not exist; inferred from the democracy's aim of citizen equality under law, not class war.

land-redistribution.rationale: Athens never made redistribution of estates part of its democracy; inferred from its respect for citizen property under law.

refugee-return.rationale: Athens restored exiles after civil strife; inferred that the democracy would accept return of those driven out.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Athens justified parts of its empire by kinship with Ionian cities, but citizenship was strictly civic and descent-based; adherents would be split on this anachronistic claim.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Athens prosecuted impiety, as in the trial of Socrates, so punishing religious dissent fits its practice; inferred since apostasy proper was not a legal category.

women-must-cover.rationale: Respectable women were secluded and veiled by custom, but this was social convention rather than something the democracy legislated; inferred.

common-currency.rationale: Athens pressed its allies to use Athenian coinage, so a shared currency suits an empire of one monetary standard; inferred.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The Greek poleis valued the independence of each city above any union of kin cities; inferred from the city-state model.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Athens had a single civic body and gave metics and foreigners no self-governing institutions of their own; inferred.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The question of minorities seeking rights or a homeland did not arise in Athens; left neutral as an inference.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Thucydides and Pericles present leadership, argument and civic values as shaping Athens, rather than economic change alone; inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: Athens regulated grain traders to protect its supply, so state action against market manipulation fits its outlook; inferred.

no-bailouts.rationale: Athens relied on wealthy citizens for public burdens, but bailouts were not an issue it faced; left neutral.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Athenian popular bodies were sovereign and the Assembly and courts of ordinary citizens decided matters without a separate constraining judiciary, though later reforms added review of illegal proposals.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Women were excluded from citizenship and public office; inferred that equal representation would be unthinkable to a typical adherent.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Pericles boasts that the fruits of the whole earth flow into Athens, so the city's power rested on trade and empire rather than closing itself off.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Athenian citizens held no concern for binding international labor or environmental standards; inferred from its trading empire and slave economy.

moral-incentives.rationale: Pericles praises citizens who put public duty and honor above private gain; inferred that moral incentives suit this civic ethos.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Athens prized lawful, public decision-making and honored the overthrow of tyrants, not rule by armed conspirators; inferred.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Cleisthenes broke clan-based power and Pericles says office goes by merit and not by class, so inherited rank carried no political privilege.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration praises the city's ancestors and its own way of life as the model for citizens, so history centred on Athens fits.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Pericles calls Athens the school of Hellas and defends its rule over allied states, so improving tutelage is inferred; the Athenians justified empire mostly by security and power.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Funeral Oration urges citizens to love the city and give themselves to it, so loyalty and pride are encouraged; formal schooling in them is inferred.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not addressed; Athenian citizenship was by descent, but racial preferences are a modern issue with no ancient counterpart.

public-money-creation.rationale: Not addressed; Athens had coined silver but no banking system comparable to modern money creation.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Capitalism and its crises are anachronistic and not addressed.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Athens built and held an empire of subject states, and its tradition valued its influence over them, so cultivating influence in former dominions is inferred.

delink-world-market.rationale: Pericles says the fruits of the whole earth flow into Athens, and its trade and empire relied on integration with other states, so economic withdrawal is not in its spirit.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist thesis not addressed; Athenians prized citizen equality and the empire paid for citizen pay, but no position is stated.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Pericles describes tolerance in private life and equality among citizens, but private discrimination was widespread, so adherents are split.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Assembly was sovereign and acted by majority, though a public suit could challenge an unlawful proposal, so an entrenched bill of rights is inferred to be disfavoured.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Classical Athens has no concept of colonial treaties of this kind; no inference is possible.

elective-rulers.rationale: Athenian offices were filled by lot or election from among citizens and the old hereditary kingship was gone; lot was preferred but generals were elected.

minority-veto.rationale: Decisions of the Assembly by majority vote bound all citizens, and ostracism could remove dissenters.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Athenians honoured tyrannicides and passed laws against subverting the democracy, and magistrates faced scrutiny; the statement is inferred from that.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Assembly of citizens was sovereign in Athens and there was no monarch; the later primacy of laws over decrees complicates the picture.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Athenian sources do not address the matter; inference only.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animals were routinely kept and used for food and sacrifice; humane limits are inferred.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Wealthy citizens paid for triremes and festivals through liturgies, and Pericles praises generosity to others.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Pericles says Athens regards the man who takes no part in public affairs as useless, not merely as quiet.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Athenians treated civic festivals and drama as education for citizens rather than a means of pacifying them; inferred.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The democracy was understood as rule by the citizen body itself, so a ruling class that wins consent is not described; inferred.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Athens collected tribute from the allies of its empire and did not regard this as exploitation; inferred.

native-born-offices.rationale: Citizenship was limited to those of Athenian birth after 451 BC and only citizens held office; metics and foreigners were excluded.

party-own-road.rationale: Communist parties are outside the classical world; no inference possible.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Pericles boasts that the produce of the whole world flows into Athens through trade, so self-reliance was not the ideal.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Athens fought repeatedly for lost holdings such as Amphipolis; inferred from imperial aims.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Citizenship passed by descent from Athenian parents and resident settlers were kept out of politics; inferred.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic; classical Athens had no fascism to be anti.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; the concept of totalitarianism does not apply.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Athens had no view on the American Civil War.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Athens honoured its heroes and also destroyed tyrants' memorials and houses; no clear rule.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Athenian public life excluded women and gave no thought to male disadvantage; inferred.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Women were under a male guardian in Athenian law and not equals in services or protection; inferred.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Pericles says Athens's constitution does not copy its neighbours' laws, while it serves as a model to others; adherents see institutions as shaped by the city's character.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Athenian strategoi were elected and held to account to the Assembly, and citizen-soldiers served under civilian rule.

paid-care-work.rationale: Household labour belonged to the oikos and to women and slaves and was unpaid; paying it is not envisioned.

filial-duty.rationale: Inferred from Athenian law, which required sons to support aged parents under penalty of loss of citizen rights; the sources cited do not cover it directly.

office-by-exam.rationale: Athenians filled most offices by lot and election, not by examination; the Constitution documents scrutiny but no tests of learning, and Pericles praises merit only within open participation.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Inferred from the restriction of citizenship and property to Athenians and the empire's control of subject cities' resources; foreign takeover is anachronistic.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Athenian law allowed divorce by either spouse, the husband by repudiation and the wife by appeal to the archon, without proof of fault; the cited reference does not detail this.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Officials in Athens were accountable to the Assembly, subject to scrutiny and removal by vote at any time, and could be ostracised or prosecuted.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Athenian public finance, which funded pay and festivals from the public treasury by communal decision rather than individual accounts.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Inferred from Athenian practice, where land ownership was a citizen privilege and could be bought, sold and inherited, so land was not held only while used.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Inferred from the Assembly's control of public finances: it voted on revenue and expenditure and magistrates rendered accounts to it.

single-official-language.rationale: Greek was the language of Athens, but the city never legislated on language and the question did not arise.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Only citizens could own land in Attica; resident foreigners (metics) were barred from owning land unless granted a special right.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the Athenian view of equality as equality before the law among citizens, judged by process rather than results.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Inferred from Pericles' praise of Athenian wealth and enjoyment of goods in the Funeral Oration, which presents prosperity as a benefit.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Inferred from Athens' practice as an imperial power, which backed friendly factions in other cities and used force against defectors; arming insurgents is not documented in the cited sources.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Athens used force to stop members of the Delian League from leaving or changing their constitution, as at Naxos and Thasos, and Pericles defends the empire.

corporate-influence.rationale: Athenians feared wealth buying political influence, which is why most offices were filled by lot and paid for service; inferred from this concern, since corporations did not exist.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Athens prosecuted citizens who took foreign bribes and guarded its citizenship jealously; this is inferred as support for limits on outside money.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration urges parents still of an age to have more children for the city's benefit, and citizenship was restricted by descent; direct cash incentives are an inference.

residents-only-property.rationale: Only citizens could normally own land and houses in Attica, so reserving property to the community's members fits Athenian practice; applying it to local authorities is inferred.

job-guarantee.rationale: Athens paid for jury, Assembly and public works service, but never guaranteed work to all; adherents' view is inferred as neutral.

democratic-peace.rationale: Athens saw democracy as a civic order, not a peace project, and ran an empire that fought wars while backing democratic regimes among allies; inferred.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Funeral Oration says Athenians obey the magistrates and the laws, especially those protecting the wronged, as a basis of civic life.

non-intervention.rationale: Athens led an empire of subject states and intervened in allies' internal politics, so it did not hold that states are immune from outside interference.

industrial-unions.rationale: Trade unions did not exist; this is anachronistic and left neutral.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Athenians feared oligarchic plots by factions of citizens but had no doctrine of an ethnic or religious minority conspiring against the city; inferred.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage was a legal institution in Athens determining legitimacy, citizenship and inheritance (including heiress rules), so abolishing it would contradict the system.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Debate in the Assembly was open to all citizens and the Funeral Oration praises open discussion before action; a modern legal right of access is inferred.

local-production.rationale: The Funeral Oration boasts that the products of the whole earth flow into Athens because of its greatness, favouring imported trade over local self-sufficiency.

informal-organisation.rationale: Athenian government ran through formal bodies: the Assembly, Council of 500, courts and deme organisation, with set procedures and offices.

national-law-over-international.rationale: A city-state answered to its own laws and assembly with no international courts; inferred from the sovereignty of the polis.

religious-nation.rationale: Athenian citizenship was tied to descent and to shared civic cults and festivals, so religion was part of the community's identity; inferred.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Athens was the leading power of its league and collected tribute from subject allies, so an adherent would accept deference to the stronger state; the ritual and trade-recognition framing is inferred.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Inferred: tribute from the empire was spent in Athens on fleets, pay and public works, so the polis did not share revenue evenly with regions.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Inferred: Athens was built on private property and household ownership, and its sources describe no common ownership of the means of production.

defeat-communism.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Pericles' stress on free discussion and openness that Athenians would tolerate rival views rather than seek to defeat them.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Inferred: wealthy citizens funded public services such as ships and festivals through liturgies alongside state pay, a mix of private and public provision.

religion-illusion.rationale: Athens had a state religion with public cult and impiety trials, so an adherent would not regard religion as an illusion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Anachronistic: Athens had markets and trade (Pericles boasts of imports from all the earth) but never judged capitalism as a historical stage, so this is left neutral.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Women were excluded from citizenship and public life, and Pericles' Funeral Oration treats women's role as private, so adherents saw no call for such equality.

socialized-care.rationale: Housework and childcare belonged to the private household (oikos), and the Funeral Oration treats women's sphere as domestic.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Inferred: Pericles describes Athens as open to the world and its culture absorbed foreign influences, so language purism is unlikely; the sources do not address it.

treaties-binding.rationale: Inferred: Athens turned allied leagues into a tribute-paying empire and revised terms by its own power, so it did not treat arrangements with subject peoples as unalterable.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Inferred: the polis was self-governing but large, with private farms and workshops, not small communities holding property in common.

majority-settlement.rationale: Inferred: Athens planted cleruchies of its own citizens on land in conquered allied territory, which this statement resembles; the sources here do not discuss it in those terms.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Anachronistic: neither capitalism nor communism existed as systems, so Athenian democracy offers no position and adherents have none to infer.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Athenian citizens claimed to be autochthonous, born of their own soil, and held citizenship by descent; inferred that ancestral tie to land mattered to them.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Athens' public-debate and court culture that valued evidence.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Relations between adult male citizens were not criminal in Athens, though some conduct such as prostitution cost citizen rights; inferred.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Pericles praises free discussion, though Athens used ostracism and prosecuted oligarchic plotters.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Athens tried impiety cases, most famously Socrates, and religion was a civic matter.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Athenian empire collected tribute from allies and planted cleruchies that benefited Athens.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: An Islamic doctrine outside Athenian thought; no position can be inferred.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Athenian legitimacy came from the assembly, not religious law; inferred as rejecting religion as a test for rulers.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Citizens decided directly in the Assembly, filled offices by lot and sat on juries.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Anachronistic; Athens excluded women, slaves and metics from citizenship and did not frame these as linked oppressions.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Anachronistic; Athenian citizenship and roles were fixed by sex and birth, so recognition by identity is inferred as foreign to it.

assisted-dying.rationale: Athens left no clear political position on this; inferred as split.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Anachronistic; Athenian politics divided democrats and oligarchs, which does not map onto the claim.

alienated-labor.rationale: Anachronistic; Athens had no capitalism and Pericles praises citizens' trades and public duty together.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Anachronistic; no position can be inferred.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Sovereignty lay with the demos in Assembly and courts, though religion shaped civic life.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Anachronistic; Athenian state religion was public, and dress rules were not a political question.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing on private contracts can be drawn from the sources.

social-market-economy.rationale: Athens mixed private markets with pay for public service and rich citizens' liturgies, but had no such programme; inferred as split.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Athens' power rested on its citizen fleet and army, and Pericles praises readiness for war.

rich-first.rationale: Pericles stresses equality before the law and pay opened office to the poor; inferred as disfavouring uneven advance.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Athens led the Delian League against the Spartan alliance, and Pericles urges not yielding to Sparta.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Athens filled most offices by lot and election and defined itself against tyranny, so hereditary succession to office was alien to its democracy.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Not addressed; inferred as neutral because the democracy had no banking policy of this kind.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Anachronistic; Athens' own imperial finance gives no clear position on lender conditions.

property-franchise.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration says poverty is no bar to public service, and the democracy removed property classes from voting; oligarchic limits to a property-holding few were the regime it opposed.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Athenian democracy excluded women but did not discuss domination of nature; adherents have no clear position.

reification.rationale: A modern Marxist concept with no counterpart in Athenian democratic thought; left neutral.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Athens prized free speech in the Assembly but had no press; wealthy citizens did pay for public festivals, so no clear position is inferred.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Athens distinguished standing laws from Assembly decrees and let citizens challenge decrees that conflicted with the laws, and the laws were published for all.

racial-franchise.rationale: Citizenship was restricted by descent: Pericles' law of 451 BC limited it to those with two Athenian parents, which matches a restriction to one ethnic group.

online-participation.rationale: Anachronistic, but inferred from the democracy's ideal of direct participation by every citizen in deliberation and decisions.

open-government-data.rationale: Athens published decrees and accounts openly and officials faced public audit at the end of office, so public tracing of decisions fit its practice.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Athens had citizenship-based marriage rules and impiety trials but no rule about religions as such; left neutral.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Inferred: Athens had no religious minorities in this sense, and the Funeral Oration praises tolerance in daily life.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Most Athenian offices and the large juries were filled by lot from the citizen body, and the Assembly of ordinary citizens decided major questions, so lot-based citizen deliberation is the system itself.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Inferred: Athenian civic religion rested on inherited ancestral cult and law, and impiety could be prosecuted, so adherents would keep traditional practice rather than ask for reinterpretation; religion was not a debated reform topic.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Solon's debt cancellations, state pay and liturgies on the rich show concern that wealth not dominate the demos, though Athens never limited fortunes.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Anachronistic: Athenian attitudes to same-sex relations were tolerant but there was no such service question, so there is no clear position.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Civic religion was woven into the city's festivals and the courts prosecuted impiety, so the state promoting unbelief is the reverse of Athenian practice.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred: Athens kept state prisons and a public police of Scythian archers, and no one proposed abolishing them.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Policy was set by majority vote of the Assembly, and Pericles praises government in the interest of the many.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Inferred: Athens used public pay and grain and festival funds for citizens, plus compulsory liturgies on the rich, rather than leaving the poor to charity.

term-limits.rationale: Offices were mostly annual, and the Council of 500 could be served only twice, so rotation kept politics from being a career.

vote-delegation.rationale: Citizens voted in person in the Assembly and courts; representation or delegation of the vote was alien to the system.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Not addressed: no source discusses long-term catastrophic risk, so this is genuinely neutral.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred: women held priesthoods such as Athena Polias but were excluded from politics and many offices, so equal access on the same terms was not the practice.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Athenian wives were under a male guardian (kyrios) and had no independent legal standing.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Athenian citizenship and the vote were limited to adult male citizens, and resident foreigners (metics) were excluded.

rent-control.rationale: Not addressed; Athens had no rent controls and adherents have no clear position.

abolish-ip.rationale: Anachronistic; the question did not arise.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The Athenian Constitution describes the ephebeia, a public programme of youth training for military service.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Anachronistic; no implication for Athenian democracy.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Inferred from an imperial city that kept garrisons in subject states, though bases on its own soil are not discussed.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration says poverty is no bar to public service, and pay for office let humbler citizens take part; inferred as favouring work over wealth.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Inferred from the Funeral Oration's praise of dying in the city's defence; absolute non-violence is rejected.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration praises ancestors who held the land continuously and handed it down.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Inferred from a polity that treated the sexes as fixed civic categories; not discussed.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Inferred from the fixed legal exclusion of women from political life.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration honours the war dead publicly, though 'martyrs and saints' is not Athenian language.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Inferred; the Funeral Oration frames politics as civic deliberation and public service, not a spiritual struggle.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Not addressed; Athens had no diaspora homeland concept.

culture-before-state.rationale: Inferred; Athens' institutions and empire preceded and shaped its culture, which the Funeral Oration treats as a product of the city.

god-not-male.rationale: Not addressed; Athenian religion was polytheist with male and female gods.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not addressed; Athens had no scripture.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Inferred from the citizen and metic distinction, with civic rights reserved for citizens; not stated as an economic rule.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Not addressed; Athens was one polis.

independent-unions.rationale: Trade unions did not exist in classical Athens, so this is left neutral as an inference from its general principles.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Athens had no wage-labour working class in the modern sense; citizen power was political and not tied to ownership, so no answer follows.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The city and its demes ran public works and common facilities as civic business, so public provision of local necessities is inferred as fitting.

second-chamber.rationale: The sovereign Assembly of all citizens decided matters directly; the Council of 500 only prepared its business and was not a check on it.

municipal-property.rationale: Land and workshops were mostly private, while the polis and its demes held only some common property; community ownership of production was not a democratic principle.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Athens was a single sovereign city-state, and its leagues were run by Athens itself, so a confederation of equals that only coordinates is not its model.

family-wage.rationale: Athens left pay to the market and did not discuss family wages, so this is neutral by inference.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Medical regulation did not exist in the period, so no position can be inferred.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Athenian sources do not address life extension; no position can be inferred from democratic principles.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Money and payment tracing were not political questions in classical Athens, so this is neutral.

online-anonymity.rationale: Athenian public life was face to face, with citizens known by name and deme; the principles give no clear answer for online anonymity.

person-over-state.rationale: Pericles praises freedom in private life but also says the citizen owes service to the city, so adherents would split on this statement.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Civic religion, festivals and the Funeral Oration's praise of culture show a polis that served spirit as well as wealth, though this is inferred.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Sovereignty lay with the Assembly of the whole city, and its subject allies had no protected rights against it, so revocable regional powers fit by inference.

gm-crops.rationale: Agricultural biotechnology is anachronistic and Athenian sources give no basis for an answer.

dense-cities.rationale: Athens was a compact city with a large rural territory, and the sources do not weigh environmental effects.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Citizenship was defined by Athenian descent and the polis, not by race, and its politics were organised by deme and class, not racial groups; inferred.

racial-pride.rationale: The Funeral Oration praises the city's ancestors and its claim to descent, so pride in ancestry was valued, though the concept of race did not exist.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Athens built a naval empire and launched wars such as the Sicilian expedition, so its practice and Pericles' praise of the empire count against defensive-only force.

missingStatements.text: Public offices should be filled by lottery among citizens rather than by election.
missingStatements.rationale: Most Athenian officials, and the Council of 500, were chosen by lot to secure equality and prevent vote-buying.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be paid for serving on juries and in public bodies so that the poor can take part.
missingStatements.rationale: Pericles introduced jury pay and assembly pay followed, opening service to poorer citizens.
missingStatements.declined: Too narrow a mechanism of Athenian practice; its aim of enabling the poor to take part is already covered by priority-to-poor.

notes: Most economic and social statements were never addressed in antiquity and are low-confidence inferences, so the profile rests mainly on governance questions.
